# Wasserstein GAN Summary
The Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) is a modification of the traditional GAN framework designed to improve the stability of training and mitigate issues such as mode collapse and vanishing gradients. WGAN replaces the original discriminator with a "critic" whose strategy set consists of functions with bounded Lipschitz norm. The objective function becomes the difference of expected critic scores between generated and reference distributions, mathematically captured as ( L_{WGAN}(\mu_G, D) = \mathbb{E} *{x\sim \mu_G}[D(x)] - \mathbb{E}* {x\sim \mu_{ref}}[D(x)] ) , and, via Kantorovich-Rubenstein duality, closely relates to the Wasserstein-1 distance. The critic provides continuous, informative gradients for the generator, even when the supports of the distributions do not overlap—a notable improvement over standard GANs, which use Jensen-Shannon divergence and often provide poor gradients when distributions are disjoint.
To train WGANs, the critic must maintain the Lipschitz constraint, which can be achieved by weight clipping, spectral normalization, or by adding a gradient penalty to the loss. These methods ensure the critic does not violate the Lipschitz constraint and help with stable training. In practice, WGANs allow for more robust convergence and reduced mode collapse compared to classic GANs, as their critic guides the generator directly towards minimizing the Wasserstein distance between real and generated data.
